query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In stainless steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, the formation of a chromium‐rich passive film—and its enhanced repair dynamics—is promoted by a high density of grain boundaries in ultrafine-grained microstructures. This microstructural feature speeds up chromium diffusion to the surface and facilitates rapid re-passivation after local disruption, thereby reducing the overall corrosion rate.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional stainless steel (e.g., 304 or duplex steel) with a relatively coarse-grained microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply severe plastic deformation (SPD) or an equivalent processing method to reduce the grain size to the ultrafine regime, while keeping the alloy composition constant.
generation.conditions: Electrochemical corrosion tests conducted in a simulated chemical-processing (e.g., chloride-containing aqueous solution) environment and, if feasible, under temperature conditions typical for nuclear power applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased density of grain boundaries in the ultrafine-grained steel.
generation.mechanism: Grain boundaries act as fast diffusion channels for chromium, enhancing the formation and repair of a protective chromium oxide passivation film at the metal-solution interface. This film minimizes active metal dissolution by dynamically self-healing in response to local chemical or mechanical disruptions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the coarse-grained baseline, the ultrafine-grained steel will exhibit a passivation film with a higher chromium concentration and a lower corrosion rate, as evidenced by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization measurements.
generation.baseline: The corrosion behavior and passive film composition of conventionally processed (coarse-grained) stainless steel under identical test conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under conditions typical for chemical processing (moderate chloride exposures, near-ambient to moderately elevated temperatures) and under controlled operational temperatures in nuclear applications. It may not apply if environmental conditions (e.g., extreme pH or temperature) compromise the integrity of the passive film regardless of microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: The contribution of other alloying elements (such as Ni, Mo, or Cu) and the influence of operational factors (like pH fluctuations and specific temperature profiles in nuclear environments) on the stability and repair kinetics of the passive film remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of steel samples with identical compositions: one group processed to obtain a conventional coarse-grained structure and another processed via SPD to achieve an ultrafine-grained structure. Expose both groups to an identical corrosive environment (e.g., 0.6 M NaCl solution) under controlled temperature conditions. Use surface characterization techniques (XPS, TEM) to analyze the passive film composition and electrochemical methods (EIS, potentiodynamic polarization) to measure corrosion rates.
measurements: Chromium concentration in the passive film (via XPS or STEM-EDS)
Corrosion current density and impedance spectra (from electrochemical testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained steel does not show a statistically significant increase in the chromium enrichment of the passive film and a corresponding decrease in corrosion rate compared to the coarse-grained steel, then the hypothesis that grain-boundary-enhanced rapid re-passivation governs corrosion resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques enable the fabrication of ultrafine-grained (UFG) or nanocrystalline (NC) materials in bulk forms suitable for load-carrying structural applications []. With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. The enhanced corrosion resistance of UFG/NC SSs compared with coarse-grained (CG) materials has been mostly attributed to greater Cr enrichment in the passivation film [,,,,,,,,], which has been validated experimentally by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [] and recently by Cs-corrected scanning-transmission electron microscopy (STEM) [,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed. cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: Cr depletion depth increased significantly in DS2205 compared to AlCoCrFeNi2.1, with an increase in temperature from 450 °C to 650 °C. At 650 °C, the Cr depletion depth for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~50 μm, while that for DS2205 was ~300 μm. This suggests that Al in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 acted as a sacrificial element and reduced Cr dissolution rate in the molten salt compared to DS2205. Redox control technique has been utilized for corrosion mitigation in molten fluoride and chloride salts []. Dissolution of Al and Cr into the molten salt resulted in the formation of AlCl3 and CrCl2, which formed a redox couple of Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2. At the redox potential, Co, Ni, and Fe become relatively nobler and their dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable. These findings suggest that Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2 couple may be used as redox buffer to slow or stop the dissolution of Fe, Co, and Ni from AlCoCrFeNi2.1 [].
